title: Plans Without Guesswork
bottom_line: plan-helper asks the open decisions your chosen level calls for, lists the rest, cuts unrequested changes, keeps changes small, and proves full coverage.

sections.heading: It runs on its own whenever Claude writes a plan

blocks.caption: It runs automatically whenever Claude writes an implementation plan. You can also invoke it directly, optionally naming the question level: everything, balanced or material.

before.label: Runs by itself
before.text: Whenever Claude writes an implementation plan, plan-helper's rules apply without you typing anything.

blocks.title: When it kicks in
items: Whenever Claude is writing, drafting, revising or presenting an implementation plan.
In plan mode, before Claude leaves plan mode (ExitPlanMode).
Inside split-plan step 1b.
When you say "plan this", "make a plan" or "how would you implement", even if you never mention plan-helper.

terms.definition: A written list of what to build and how, step by step, before any code is written.
One atomic thing you requested, quoted word for word and numbered A1, A2 and so on.
A table in the plan with one row per ask, showing which step delivers it and how it is checked.
Whoever builds the plan afterwards, which may be a Claude subagent.
How many open decisions come back to you as questions: everything, balanced or material.
The plan's list of decisions Claude made itself because your level did not ask them, each with its reason.

sections.heading: You pick how many decisions come back to you

blocks.title: The three question levels
rows: `everything`
Every decision neither your request nor the code settles.
Nothing.
`balanced`

Anything you will see or experience (layout, wording, placement, interactions, behaviour, user-facing edge cases), and anything costly to undo (data shape, migration, new dependency, public API, security, size of the change).
Internal details: naming, file structure, internal error handling, test layout.
`material`
Only choices that send the work in a different direction or cannot be cheaply undone: architecture, data model and migration, scope, public API, security, billing.
Everything else, including small UX details.

blocks.title: How the level works
items: The level is the first question, unless you pass it as an argument (`/plan-tools:plan-helper material`), a calling skill such as create-webapp already asked it, or Claude is revising a plan that records it.
When Claude decides, it takes the answer the existing code points to, or else the option it would have recommended.
Every decision Claude makes is listed in the plan under Assumed decisions, so you can veto it at review, and the list is copied into the PR body.
A vague ask, and whether to include something that serves no ask, are asked at every level.
Implementers use the plan's level for decisions that come up while they work: below its bar they decide and add to Assumed decisions, above it they stop and ask.
A subagent given no level uses `everything`.

sections.heading: It exists to stop four ways a plan goes wrong

cards.title: Ask, not assume
cards.text: Problem: Claude filled gaps with its own decisions, and they were not yours.

points.text: Each open decision is asked, or listed under Assumed decisions, as your level says.

cards.title: No unrequested changes
cards.text: Problem: the PR held changes you could not connect to anything you asked for.

points.text: Each step cites the ask it serves (`Serves: A<n>`).
Anything without one is cut or asked about.

cards.title: Smallest complete change
cards.text: Problem: the change was bigger than needed.

points.text: Each step says why nothing smaller works. Real smaller-or-larger choices come to you as questions.

cards.title: Cover everything
cards.text: Problem: after all the testing and review, the result still missed parts, looked bad or was awkward to use.

points.text: A requirement map lists each ask word for word.
Each ask shows the step that delivers it and how it is checked.

blocks.caption: Each card is a past failure and the rule plan-helper uses against it.

blocks.text: Plans that looked fine still produced the wrong result. The checks include running the real app or command, not only tests.

sections.heading: Claude works through six steps before you see the plan

steps.title: Pick the question level
steps.text: From your argument, the calling skill or the plan being revised, or else asked as the first question: everything, balanced or material.

steps.title: Capture the asks
steps.text: Claude splits your request into atomic asks, quoting your words exactly (A1, A2, …). A vague ask such as "make it nicer" becomes a question in itself.

steps.title: Read the code
steps.text: Everything the asks touch: callers, tests, fixtures, config, and existing helpers and patterns.

steps.title: Ask the open decisions your level calls for
steps.text: A decision is open when neither your request nor the existing code settles it. When Claude is unsure whether something is a decision, it treats it as one. Your level decides which are asked; Claude decides the rest and lists them.

steps.title: Write the plan
steps.text: With its question level, a requirement map, a decisions list, an assumed decisions list, the steps, how to verify, and the implementation rules.

steps.title: Audit, then present
steps.text: Claude rereads the plan against every rule and fixes what fails. The plan is not ready to show you until this passes.

blocks.title: What counts as an open decision
items: UX: layout, wording, placement, interactions
Behaviour
Edge cases
Naming
Data shape
Libraries
File structure
Error handling
Migration

sections.heading: You answer short multiple-choice questions, in plain English

items.label: options per question
items.note: recommendation first, with a one-line reason

blocks.title: How the questions are written
items: Asked through AskUserQuestion, as many rounds as needed.

Questions, options and descriptions are full, plain English, never a compressed style, even if one is active. If the humanizer plugin is available, Claude runs /humanizer:humanizer on the question text first.
Each question stands on its own, since you may only see the dialog: it names the thing and says what Claude found if that matters.
Concrete options, with Claude's recommendation first, marked "(Recommended)".
Where there is a real smaller-or-larger choice, such as reusing an existing component or making a new one, or patching one screen or all of them, you get both options and what each covers.
No placeholder answer with "we can change it later". Claude waits for your answer.
Decisions that come up later, while writing or auditing, follow the same level: the ones it asks come back to you the same way, and Claude decides and lists the rest.

sections.heading: Each step names the ask it serves and why that size

blocks.title: Sections every plan contains
rows: Question level
A `Question level:` line naming the level: `everything`, `balanced` or `material`. Implementers use the same bar for decisions that come up while they work.
Requirement map
One row per ask, with columns Ask (verbatim), Delivered by (step), Verified by, and Status. Status starts as `[ ]`; implementers tick it to `[x]` once the ask is delivered and verified.
Decisions
Every answer you gave, as `question → user's answer`. Implementers follow these and never decide them again.
Assumed decisions
Every decision Claude made itself because your level did not ask it, as `decision → choice — one-line reason`. Empty at `everything`. It is copied into the PR body.
Steps
For each step: the files and what changes in each, `Serves: A<n>`, and `Why this size:`, saying why no smaller change works.
Verification
Tests, plus running the real app or command and trying each ask the way you will use it. It names exactly what to run and check for each ask.
Implementation rules
A fixed block, copied word for word, that binds whoever builds the plan.

blocks.text: Trying each ask the way you will use it means clicking through the UI, running the CLI, or opening the page at the right screen size.
For `Why this size:`, reuse of existing code beats new code, and a one-line change beats a new abstraction. "It's cleaner" or "while we're here" are not reasons.

blocks.summary: The implementation rules block, all 6 rules

blocks.code:
## Implementation rules

- Change only what a step in this plan lists. Every changed line must trace to an ask in the requirement map. No drive-by refactors, renames, reformatting, dependency bumps, or "while I'm here" fixes — note them in the final report instead.
- Follow the Decisions section exactly. If you hit a decision this plan doesn't answer, use the plan's question level (`everything` if it names none). If the level would not ask it, pick the answer the existing code points to (else the one you would recommend) and add it to the plan's Assumed decisions (in a split plan, in `.planning/SPEC.md`). If the level would ask it, stop and ask the user (AskUserQuestion) — don't pick one yourself. If you are a subagent and can't ask the user directly, end your run with the question as your final report (plain English, 2–4 options, your recommendation first); the parent will ask the user and send you the answer so you can continue.
- When you raise the PR, copy the plan's Assumed decisions into the PR body under an "Assumed decisions" heading, so reviewers see every choice the user did not make.
- Tick each requirement map row's Status once it is delivered and verified. In a split plan, tick your session's rows in `.planning/SPEC.md`.
- Keep each change as small as it can be while still complete. Reuse existing code and patterns before writing new ones.
- Done means every requirement map row assigned to your work (the whole plan, or your session's rows) is delivered and verified — including running the real app/command per the Verification section, not only tests.
blocks.caption: split-plan copies this block into every session file.

sections.heading: Before presenting, the plan is checked against every rule

cards.title: Coverage
cards.text: Every ask has a row, a step that delivers it and a real-use check. No ask is silently dropped or narrowed.

cards.title: No unrequested changes
cards.text: Every step and file has a `Serves:` pointing at a real ask.

cards.title: Size
cards.text: Could less code, fewer files or reuse do the same job? Claude shrinks it. A real trade-off is asked if your level calls for it, else listed as assumed.

cards.title: No unlisted decisions
cards.text: Every choice is in Decisions, settled by the code, or in Assumed decisions and below your level's bar. Anything else becomes a question.

cards.title: Rules block present
cards.text: The implementation rules block is there, word for word.

blocks.text: Something that seems needed but serves no ask, such as a bug Claude found, is asked about instead of included.
Then Claude presents the plan. In plan mode that means leaving plan mode (ExitPlanMode), unless a calling skill such as split-plan says to present later.

reference.title: About the plan-tools plugin
items: Plugin purpose: plan-driven workflow tools that bootstrap a new web or mobile app end to end, split implementation plans into context-sized resumable sessions, and drive them to PRs.
Installing plan-tools also installs the plugins it depends on: `ntfy`, `fastapi-template` and `htmx-vs-alpine`.

No environment variables are needed. The one setting, `designer_ui_review` (default `false`), is changed with `/plugin configure plan-tools@wovemind`. It runs the ui-change-guard designer review (/ui-change-guard:review-ui-change) before finalize-pr raises a PR.
